## Defining functions to save plots in multiple formats
```{r, include=FALSE}
# Define output paths
output_dir <- "1.DEAnalysis/figures"
formats <- c("png", "pdf", "svg", "tiff")

# Create directories if they don’t exist
for (fmt in formats) {
  dir.create(file.path(output_dir, fmt), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
}

# Function to save plots in multiple formats
save_plot <- function(plot, filename, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 600) {
  for (fmt in formats) {
    ggsave(
      filename = file.path(output_dir, fmt, paste0(filename, ".", fmt)),
      plot = plot, 
      width = width, height = height, dpi = dpi
    )
  }
}

```
Here I'm using the Data Carpentry tutorial on RNAseq data analysis
https://scienceparkstudygroup.github.io/rna-seq-lesson/05-descriptive-plots/index.html

## Creating a DESeq object with original count data 

Since we have 3’ tagged RNA-seq(QuantSeq) data it's appropriate to use orignal count data instead of TPM
Thread on salmon counts for DESeq2, TagSeq data doesn't need to be corrected for gene length. 
Instead we need to use the original counts, e.g. txi$counts as a counts matrix, e.g. providing to DESeqDataSetFromMatrix or to the edgeR or limma functions without calculating an offset and without using countsFromAbundance.
https://bioconductor.org/packages/devel/bioc/vignettes/tximport/inst/doc/tximport.html#Downstream_DGE_in_Bioconductor

```{r DE import counts}
#Count data from Star-Salmon using Nextflow RNASeq pipeline
counts_file  <- "Results_nf_pipelines/Results_all72_nfcore_day2/star_salmon/salmon.merged.gene_counts.tsv"
starsalmon_counts <- read.delim(counts_file, header = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

## Check that sample names match in both files
#select all columns except the first two
all(colnames(starsalmon_counts[, -c(1,2)]) %in% sampledata$sample)
#check if they are in the same order
all(colnames(starsalmon_counts[, -c(1,2)]) == sampledata$sample)
#they are not in the same order

#add rownames to the sampledata
rownames(sampledata) <- sampledata$sample  #rownames are the sample, as the colnames in the count data
#add rownames to the count data
rownames(starsalmon_counts) <- starsalmon_counts$gene_id
starsalmon_counts_sub <- starsalmon_counts[, -c(1,2)]

# Reorder sampledata to match the order of starsalmon_counts columns
sampledataord <- sampledata[match(colnames(starsalmon_counts[, -c(1, 2)]), sampledata$sample), ]

# Check if they are now in the same order
all(colnames(starsalmon_counts[, -c(1, 2)]) == sampledataord$sample)

#Round counts to integers
starsalmon_counts_sub <- round(starsalmon_counts_sub)

# Write the counts to a file with row names as the first column
# write.table(
#  starsalmon_counts_sub, 
#  file = "1.DEAnalysis/data/starsalmoncounts_alltissues.txt", 
#  sep = "\t", 
#  quote = FALSE, 
#  row.names = TRUE,  # Ensures row names are written as the first column

# )

# Load the RDS file
summarized_experiment <- readRDS("Results_nf_pipelines/Results_all72_nfcore_day2/star_salmon/salmon.merged.gene_counts.SummarizedExperiment.rds")
#scaled_summexp <- readRDS("Results_nf_pipelines/Results_all72_nfcore_day2/star_salmon/salmon.merged.gene_counts_scaled.SummarizedExperiment.rds")
# View the loaded object
summarized_experiment
#scaled_summexp

# List assay names
assayNames(summarized_experiment)
#assayNames(scaled_summexp)

head(assay(summarized_experiment, "salmon.merged.gene_counts"))
#head(assay(scaled_summexp, "salmon.merged.gene_counts_scaled"))

starsalmon_counts_sumexp <- assay(summarized_experiment, "salmon.merged.gene_counts")
#round
starsalmon_counts_sumexp <- round(starsalmon_counts_sumexp)
any(is.na(starsalmon_counts_sumexp))

#starsalmon_counts_sub and starsalmon_counts_sumexp are the same, I just loaded one directly from the tsv and other from the rds file
```

### Important note about using counts and not scaled counts for QuantSeq data:
From Nexflow pipeline: https://nf-co.re/rnaseq/3.14.0/docs/output/
Use bias uncorrected counts: load and use the txi$counts matrix (or salmon.merged.gene_counts.tsv) with DESeq2. This does not correct for potential differential isoform usage. Alternatively, if you have 3’ tagged RNA-seq data this is the most suitable method.
That's why I'm using the original counts and not the scaled counts for DESeq2 analysis.

```{r}
#Counts is appropriate for TagSeq data
#https://bioconductor.org/packages/devel/bioc/vignettes/tximport/inst/doc/tximport.html#3%E2%80%99_tagged_RNA-seq
#If you have 3’ tagged RNA-seq data, then correcting the counts for gene length will induce a bias in your analysis, because the counts do not have length bias. Instead of using the default full-transcript-length pipeline, we recommend to use the original counts, e.g. txi$counts as a counts matrix, e.g. providing to DESeqDataSetFromMatrix or to the edgeR or limma functions without calculating an offset and without using countsFromAbundance.

## Create DESeq object from counts 
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = starsalmon_counts_sumexp, 
                              colData = sampledataord, 
                              design = ~Sample_ID)

dds
```

## Variance stabilization of counts
This step here is to visualize the variance stabilization step and to make the PCA plot with stabilized counts. 
Normalization is automatically performed by DESeq2 when running the DESeq() function.
```{r counts stabilization}

# Variance stabilization
# Plot of mean - sd comparison
# Variance - mean plot for all genes
p_mean_sd_scaled <- 
  starsalmon_counts_sub %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  rownames_to_column("gene") %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = - gene, names_to = "sample", values_to = "counts") %>% 
  group_by(gene) %>% 
  summarise(gene_average = mean(counts), gene_stdev = sd(counts)) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  ggplot(., aes(x = log10(gene_average), y = log10(gene_stdev))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, fill = "grey", colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Gene count average (log10 scale)",
       y = "Gene count standard deviation (log10 scale)") +
  ggtitle("Mean - Standard deviation relationship\n(no variance stabilization ")
p_mean_sd_scaled
#ggsave(plot = p_mean_sd_scaled, "figures/novarstabilized.png", dpi = 600, units = "in", height = 4, width = 5)


# Variance stabilization
# estimation of size factors and dispersions are required before performing the variance stabilization

dds = estimateSizeFactors(dds)

dds = estimateDispersions(object = dds, 
	                      fitType = "parametric", 
	                      quiet = TRUE)

vsd = varianceStabilizingTransformation(object = dds, blind = TRUE, fitType = "parametric") # do not take the design formula into account, best practice for sample-level QC
 
# extract the matrix of variance stabilised counts
variance_stabilised_counts <- assay(vsd)

# create the mean-sd plot
p_mean_sd_vst <- 
  variance_stabilised_counts %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  rownames_to_column("gene") %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = - gene, names_to = "sample", values_to = "counts") %>% 
  group_by(gene) %>% 
  summarise(gene_average = mean(counts), gene_stdev = sd(counts)) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  ggplot(., aes(x = gene_average, y = gene_stdev)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, fill = "grey", colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Gene count average (variance stabilised)", 
       y = "Gene count standard deviation (variance stabilised)") +
  ggtitle("Mean - Standard deviation relationship\n(after variance stabilization ")

p_mean_sd_vst
#ggsave(plot = p_mean_sd_vst, "figures/varstabilized.png", dpi = 600, units = "in", height = 4, width = 5)
```

## PCA plot using variance stabilized counts

```{r PCA function}
# define a custom R function called "mypca()"

mypca <- function(x, center = TRUE, scale = TRUE){
  # Samples should be in rows
  # Variables in the columns

  # remove constant variables
  constant_val = apply(x,2,'sd')
  x_reduced = x[,constant_val>0]
  
  # perform SVD
  SVD <- svd(scale(x_reduced,center = center, scale = scale))
  
  # create scores data frame
  scores <- as.data.frame(SVD$u %*% diag(SVD$d))
  rownames(scores) <- rownames(x)
  colnames(scores) <- paste0("PC", c(1:dim(scores)[2]))
  
  # create loadings data frams
  loadings <- data.frame(SVD$v)
  colnames(loadings) <- paste0("PC", c(1:dim(loadings)[2]))
  rownames(loadings) <- colnames(x_reduced)
  
  # create data frame for explained variances
  explained_var <- as.data.frame(round((SVD$d^2) / sum(SVD$d^2)*100, digits = 1))
  rownames(explained_var) <- paste0("PC", c(1:dim(loadings)[2]))
  colnames(explained_var) <- "exp_var"
  
  # return result
  return (list("scores" = scores, "loadings" = loadings, "explained_var" = explained_var))
}
```

## PCA plots for each subset colored by genotype, tissue and day
```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(ggConvexHull)
library(ggnewscale)
library(forcats)

# Define the fixed tissue order and corresponding colors
tissue_levels <- c("Leaf", "Hypocotyl", "RootCrown",
                   "MatureBranchedZoneTaproot", "YoungBranchedZoneTaproot", 
                   "AUZTaproot", "AUZBasalRoots", "RootTipTaproot", "RootTipBasalRoots")

# Assign colors explicitly (ensuring they are always in the correct order)
tissue_palette <- setNames(my_pal_RDGA_leaf, tissue_levels)

# Define color palettes for variables
geno_palette <- c("brown4", "burlywood") # Genotype colors
day_palette <- c("grey70", "black", "forestgreen") # Day colors

# Function to create PCA plots
create_pca_plot <- function(scores_df, explained_var, color_by, shape_by, color_palette, subset_name) {
  
  p <- ggplot(scores_df, aes(PC1, PC2)) +
    geom_point(aes_string(color = color_by, shape = shape_by), size = 4, show.legend = TRUE) +
    scale_color_manual(values = color_palette) +  # Ensures colors follow the fixed order
    xlab(paste0("PC1: ", explained_var[1], "% variance")) +
    ylab(paste0("PC2: ", explained_var[2], "% variance")) +
    coord_fixed(ratio = 1) +
    theme_classic() +
    theme(
      axis.title = element_text(size = 24),
      legend.title = element_text(size = 18),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 18),
      legend.position = "none"
    ) +
    guides(
      color = guide_legend(title = color_by),
      shape = guide_legend(title = shape_by)
    )
  
  # Save plot using your function
  save_plot(p, paste0("pca_", subset_name, "_col", color_by, "_", shape_by))
  
  return(p)
}

# Function to generate PCA plots for each subset
generate_pca_plots <- function(subset_name, sample_ids, color_by, shape_by, color_palette) {
  
  cat("Processing:", subset_name, "\n")
  
  # Filter expression matrix
  subset_counts <- t_variance_stabilised_counts[sample_ids, , drop = FALSE]
  
  if (nrow(subset_counts) < 2) {
    cat("Skipping", subset_name, "- Not enough samples for PCA\n")
    return(NULL)
  }

  pca_results <- mypca(subset_counts, center = TRUE, scale = TRUE)
  scores <- pca_results$scores
  
  # Explained variance
  explained_variance <- pca_results$explained_var %>% pull("exp_var")
  
  # Join with metadata
  scores_with_conditions <- scores %>%
    rownames_to_column("sample") %>%
    left_join(sampledata, by = "sample")

  # Ensure Tissue is a factor with the correct order
  scores_with_conditions <- scores_with_conditions %>%
    mutate(Tissue = factor(Tissue, levels = tissue_levels))

  # Adjust only tissue_palette dynamically, leave other palettes untouched
  adjusted_palette <- color_palette
  if (color_by == "Tissue") {
    subset_tissues <- levels(scores_with_conditions$Tissue)
    adjusted_palette <- tissue_palette[subset_tissues] # Keep order & colors fixed
  }

  # Generate plots
  plot <- create_pca_plot(scores_with_conditions, explained_variance, color_by, shape_by, adjusted_palette, subset_name)
  
  return(plot)
}

# Generate PCA plots for all subsets
pca_plots <- list()
for (subset_name in names(subsets)) {
  sample_ids <- subsets[[subset_name]]
  
  # Create genotype-based PCA
  pca_plots[[paste0(subset_name, "_geno")]] <- generate_pca_plots(subset_name, sample_ids, "Genotype", "Day", geno_palette)
  
  # Create tissue-based PCA
  pca_plots[[paste0(subset_name, "_tissue")]] <- generate_pca_plots(subset_name, sample_ids, "Tissue", "Day", tissue_palette)
  
  # Create day-based PCA
  pca_plots[[paste0(subset_name, "_day")]] <- generate_pca_plots(subset_name, sample_ids, "Day", "Day", day_palette)
}
```

## Differential expression analysis
First will call the DESeq function on a DESeqDataSet object that you’ve just created under the name dds. 
It will be returned under the same R object name dds.
Then, results are extracted using the results function on the dds object and results will be extracted as a table under the name res (short for results).

## Genotype main effect, Stampede vs. Red Hawk, regardless of day
Stampede vs. Red Hawk means that we are comparing the fold change of Stampede with respect to Red Hawk.
Red Hawk is the reference level, so the fold change will be calculated as Stampede/Red Hawk.
The fold change will be positive if Stampede is higher than Red Hawk, and negative if Stampede is lower than Red Hawk.

```{r DE analysis}
## Create DESeq object from counts 
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = starsalmon_counts_sumexp, 
                              colData = sampledataord, 
                              design = ~Sample_ID)
dds
#DESeq2 recommends using variance-stabilizing transformation (VST) or rlog transformation instead of raw counts for visualization.vsd
                             
dds <- DESeq(dds)
```

## Heatmap of sample to sample distances

```{r}
##Heatmap of sample to sample distances 
# Load necessary libraries
library(pheatmap)
library(RColorBrewer)
library(scales)  # For showing colors
library(grDevices)

#using the Variance Stabilizing Transformation (vsd object created above)
sampleDists <- dist(t(assay(vsd)))  
sampleDistMatrix <- as.matrix(sampleDists)
 
#rownames(sampleDistMatrix) <- vsd$Sample_ID
#colnames(sampleDistMatrix) <- rownames(sampleDistMatrix)


colors <- colorRampPalette( rev(brewer.pal(9, "Blues")) )(255)
pheatmap(sampleDistMatrix,
         clustering_distance_rows = sampleDists,
         clustering_distance_cols = sampleDists,
         col = colors)

# Ensure the tissue palette is assigned correctly
tissue_palette <- setNames(my_pal_RDGA_leaf, tissue_levels)

day_palette <- c("day2" = "grey70", "day5" = "black", "day7" = "forestgreen")
geno_palette <- c("RedHawk" = "brown4", "Stampede" = "burlywood")

# Define metadata annotation colors (using your predefined palettes)
metadata_roots_ann_colors <- list(
  Day = day_palette,  # Uses predefined day_palette
  Genotype = geno_palette,  # Uses predefined geno_palette
  Tissue = tissue_palette  # Uses predefined tissue_palette
)
##Here important to have the same order of the columns in the metadata and the rows in the heatmap
##Here I need to use sampledataord instead of sampledata
# Create annotation dataframe (Make sure row names match heatmap column names)
annotation_col <- data.frame(
  Day = sampledataord$Day,  
  Genotype = sampledataord$Genotype,
  Tissue = sampledataord$Tissue
)

colnames(sampleDistMatrix)
rownames(annotation_col)

# Ensure row names align with heatmap column names
rownames(annotation_col) <- colnames(assay(vsd))  

library(ArchR)
paletteLength <- 50
#this palette is red to white to blue because smaller distances are more similar, so we want them to be red
myColor <- colorRampPalette(c("red", "white", "blue"))(paletteLength)


# Ensure unique breaks
min_value <- min(sampleDistMatrix)
max_value <- max(sampleDistMatrix)

# Check if min_value is positive; adjust scaling if necessary
if (min_value >= 0) {
  # If all values are positive, shift the center to the mean
  midpoint <- mean(sampleDistMatrix)  
} else {
  # Otherwise, use zero as the center
  midpoint <- 0
}

# Generate unique breakpoints for proper scaling
myBreaks <- seq(min_value, max_value, length.out = paletteLength)

# Generate the heatmap with proper annotations
pheatmap(sampleDistMatrix,
         annotation_col = annotation_col,
         annotation_colors = metadata_roots_ann_colors,  # Apply annotation colors
         clustering_distance_rows = sampleDists,
         clustering_distance_cols = sampleDists,
         color = myColor,
         breaks = myBreaks,# Heatmap color scale
         )

print(colnames(sampleDistMatrix))  # Check column names of heatmap matrix
print(rownames(annotation_col))  # Check row names of annotations
head(annotation_col)  # Check annotation data

# Ensure Tissue is a factor with the correct order
annotation_col$Tissue <- factor(annotation_col$Tissue, levels = tissue_levels)

# Order the sample names based on the tissue order
ordered_samples <- rownames(annotation_col)[order(annotation_col$Tissue)]

# Ensure ordered_samples exist in sampleDistMatrix
ordered_samples <- ordered_samples[ordered_samples %in% colnames(sampleDistMatrix)]

# Reorder both rows and columns in the matrix and annotation data
sampleDistMatrix <- sampleDistMatrix[ordered_samples, ordered_samples]
annotation_col <- annotation_col[ordered_samples, ]


# Generate the heatmap with proper annotations & ordered columns
pheatmap(sampleDistMatrix,
         annotation_col = annotation_col,
         annotation_colors = metadata_roots_ann_colors,  
         clustering_distance_rows = sampleDists,
         cluster_cols = FALSE,  # Disable clustering to keep the order
         color = myColor,
         breaks = myBreaks,  
         show_colnames = FALSE,  # Hide sample labels
         )
#####

#Heatmap with annotations in both rows and columns

# Create row annotations (same as columns)
annotation_row <- annotation_col  # Ensures row order matches column order

# Generate the heatmap with both row and column annotations (no clustering)
heatmap_sampledist <- pheatmap(sampleDistMatrix,
         annotation_col = annotation_col,  # Column annotations
         annotation_row = annotation_row,  # Row annotations (same order)
         annotation_colors = metadata_roots_ann_colors,  
         cluster_rows = FALSE,  # Disable row clustering
         cluster_cols = FALSE,  # Disable column clustering
         color = myColor,
         breaks = myBreaks,  
         show_colnames = FALSE,  # Hide sample labels
         show_rownames = FALSE,  # Hide row labels
         border_color = NA)
heatmap_sampledist 
#save plot with save_plot function and changing dimensions
save_plot(heatmap_sampledist, "heatmap_sampledist_square", width = 5.8, height = 3.64)
```

#3. Extract only replicate PCCs from the heatmap matrix:
#by Sample ID
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(tidyr)

# Full sample-to-sample PCC matrix from vst values
roots_sampleCorrMatrix <- cor(assay(vsd_roots), method = "pearson")

# Sample metadata
sample_info <- as.data.frame(colData(vsd_roots)) %>%
  mutate(sample = colnames(assay(vsd_roots)))

# Extract PCCs between replicates for each Sample_ID and summarize
replicate_pcc_summary <- sample_info %>%
  dplyr::group_by(Sample_ID) %>%
  dplyr::filter(n() > 1) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(
    replicate_pairs = list(combn(sample, 2, simplify = FALSE)),
    PCCs = list(map_dbl(replicate_pairs[[1]], ~ roots_sampleCorrMatrix[.x[1], .x[2]])),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    n_pairs = lengths(PCCs),
    mean_PCC = map_dbl(PCCs, mean),
    sd_PCC = map_dbl(PCCs, sd),
    min_PCC = map_dbl(PCCs, min),
    max_PCC = map_dbl(PCCs, max)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(Sample_ID, n_pairs, mean_PCC, sd_PCC, min_PCC, max_PCC)

# View table
replicate_pcc_summary

# Save the summary table
write.csv(replicate_pcc_summary, "1.DEAnalysis/output/replicate_pcc_summary_roots.csv", row.names = FALSE)

# Summary across all Sample_IDs
replicate_pcc_overall_summary <- replicate_pcc_summary %>%
  dplyr::summarise(
    total_sample_ids = n(),
    total_pairs = sum(n_pairs),
    mean_of_means = mean(mean_PCC),
    sd_of_means = sd(mean_PCC),
    overall_min_PCC = min(min_PCC),
    overall_max_PCC = max(max_PCC)
  )

# View result
replicate_pcc_overall_summary
# Save overall summary
write.csv(replicate_pcc_overall_summary, "1.DEAnalysis/output/replicate_pcc_overall_summary_roots.csv", row.names = FALSE)

```{r}
# Define your specific order for the clusters
# For example, if you want to order clusters 
#specific_order <- c(2, 3, 1, 4)

# Custom clustering function to reorder columns
custom_clustering <- function(hclust_obj, mat) {
  # Number of clusters
  k <- 4
  
  # Cut the dendrogram into k clusters
  clusters <- cutree(hclust_obj, k)
  
  # Reorder the columns based on the clusters
  order <- order(clusters)
  
  # Return the reordered dendrogram
  as.hclust(reorder(hclust_obj, order))
}
```

# Differential expression analysis: Genotype within day

# Day 3: Red Hawk vs Stampede

### Note on factor levels: 
By default, R will choose a reference level for factors based on alphabetical order. Then, if you never tell the DESeq2 functions which level you want to compare against (e.g. which level represents the control group), the comparisons will be based on the alphabetical order of the levels. 
There are two solutions: you can either explicitly tell results which comparison to make using the contrast argument (this will be shown later), or you can explicitly set the factors levels. 
In order to see the change of reference levels reflected in the results names, you need to either run DESeq or nbinomWaldTest/nbinomLRT after the re-leveling operation. 
Setting the factor levels can be done in two ways, either using factor or relevel:

```{r  d3RvsS}  
ddsExp$Exp
ddsExp$Exp  <- relevel(ddsExp$Exp, ref = "day_3_taproot_LAUZ_Stampede")
ddsExp$Exp # Now the first level is: 4 Levels: day_3_taproot_LAUZ_Stampede

#Need to run DeSeq again after leveling the factors
ddsExp <- DESeq(ddsExp)

res <- results(ddsExp)
head(res)
resultsNames(ddsExp)

all_genes_results <- results(ddsExp, contrast = c("Exp",                      # name of the factor
                                  "day_3_root_tips_taproot_Redhawk",    # name of the numerator level for fold change
                                  "day_3_root_tips_taproot_Stampede"))  # name of the denominator level  (this is the reference level)
all_equal(res, all_genes_results)

#Extracting the table of differential genes
head(all_genes_results)                
mcols(all_genes_results)

# False discovery rates

library(dplyr)

# threshold of p = 0.01
all_genes_results %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  filter(padj < 0.01) %>% 
  dim()

# threshold of p = 0.001
all_genes_results %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  filter(padj < 0.001) %>% 
  dim()

  # distribution of adjusted p-values
hist(all_genes_results$padj, col="lightblue", main = "Adjusted p-value distribution")

# distribution of non-adjusted p-values
hist(all_genes_results$pvalue, col="grey", main = "Non-adjusted p-value distribution")
```
This is 1577 differentially expressed genes at 0.01 and 1003 at 0.001 which corresponds to respectively ~5% and ~3% of the whole number transcriptome (total number of mRNA is 27,416).

## Shrinkage of log2 fold changes
Note on shrinkage of log2 fold changes from Mike Love (DESeq2 developer): https://support.bioconductor.org/p/77461/#77466

I'd recommend to use type="apeglm". The shrinkage is generally useful, which is why it is enabled by default. Full methods are described in the DESeq2 paper (see DESeq2 citation), but in short, it looks at the largest fold changes that are not due to low counts and uses these to inform a prior distribution. So the large fold changes from genes with lots of statistical information are not shrunk, while the imprecise fold changes are shrunk. This allows you to compare all estimated LFC across experiments, for example, which is not really feasible without the use of a prior.

One case where I would not use it, is if it is expected that nearly all genes will have no change and there is little to no variation across replicates (so near technical replication), and then say < 10 genes with very large fold changes. This scenario could occur in non-biological samples, for example technical replicates plus DE spike ins. The reason this would cause a problem is that the prior is formed according to a high percentile of the large fold changes, but it could miss if there were singular DE genes, and form a prior which is not wide enough to accommodate very large fold changes. It is trivial to turn off the prior in this case (betaPrior=FALSE).

The difference between results() and lfcShrink() is that the former does not provide fold change shrinkage. The latter function calls results() internally to create the p-value and adjusted p-value columns, which provide inference on the maximum likelihood LFC. The shrunken fold changes are useful for ranking genes by effect size and for visualization.
```{r  d3RvsS shrinkage}
#if (!require("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
#    install.packages("BiocManager")

#BiocManager::install("apeglm")

resultsNames(ddsExp)
resLFC_tipd3RvsS <- lfcShrink(dds = ddsExp, 
                  res = all_genes_results,
                  type = "apeglm",
                  coef = "Exp_day_3_root_tips_taproot_Redhawk_vs_day_3_root_tips_taproot_Stampede") # name or number of the coefficient (LFC) to shrink

```

# Day within genotype

# Red Hawk: day 5 vs day 3

The fold change of day 5 with respect to day 3. This is the inverse of the day 3 vs day 5 contrast, and will have the same results but with the sign of the log2 fold change reversed.
This is using day 3 as a reference level, so the fold change is calculated as day 5 / day 3.

```{r  Rhd5vsd3}

#This is 2843 differentially expressed genes at 0.01 and 1756 at 0.001 which corresponds to respectively ~5% and ~3% of the whole number transcriptome (total number of mRNA is 27,416).
```

# Heatmap of differentially expressed genes

Function to scale the raw counts
import custom function
copy-paste and execute this code in your console to get the mor_normalization() function

```{r  mor_normalization}
mor_normalization = function(data){
  library(dplyr)
  library(tibble)

  # take the log
  log_data = log(data) 
  
  # find the psuedo-references per sample by taking the geometric mean
  log_data = log_data %>% 
               rownames_to_column('gene') %>% 
               mutate (gene_averages = rowMeans(log_data)) %>% 
               filter(gene_averages != "-Inf")
  
  # the last columns is the pseudo-reference column 
  pseudo_column = ncol(log_data)
  
  # where to stop before the pseudo column 
  before_pseduo = pseudo_column - 1
  
  # find the ratio of the log data to the pseudo-reference
  ratios = sweep(log_data[,2:before_pseduo], 1, log_data[,pseudo_column], "-")
  
  # find the median of the ratios
  sample_medians = apply(ratios, 2, median)
  
  # convert the median to a scaling factor
  scaling_factors = exp(sample_medians)
  
  # use scaling factors to scale the original data
  manually_normalized = sweep(data, 2, scaling_factors, "/")
  return(manually_normalized)
}
```

```{r  raw counts viz}
# scale the raw counts
head(txi.salmon$counts)
salmon_counts_df <- as.data.frame(txi.salmon$counts)
head(salmon_counts_df)
colnames(salmon_counts_df)
scaled_counts <- mor_normalization(salmon_counts_df)
head(scaled_counts)

# Plots to compare scaled and unscaled counts
long_scaled_counts = 
  scaled_counts %>% 
  rownames_to_column("gene") %>% 
  pivot_longer(-gene, names_to = "sample", values_to = "counts") %>% 
  mutate(scaled = "yes")

long_raw_counts = 
  salmon_counts_df %>% 
  rownames_to_column("gene") %>% 
  pivot_longer(-gene, names_to = "sample", values_to = "counts") %>% 
  mutate(scaled = "no")

long_raw_and_scaled_counts = bind_rows(long_raw_counts, long_scaled_counts)

ggplot(long_raw_and_scaled_counts, 
       aes(x = scaled, y = counts + 1, fill = scaled)) +
  geom_violin() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Gene counts scaled/normalised?", y = "Gene counts (raw or scaled)")
```

## Heatmap of differentially expressed genes
### Stampede: day 5 vs day 3 volcano plot
The heatmaps below are based on the differentially expressed genes for the comparison of Stampede: day 5 vs day 3.

```{r  heatmap}
counts_normalised_only_diff_genes = 
  mor_normalization(salmon_counts_df) %>%             # normalize the counts using our custom function
  rownames_to_column("genes") %>%               
  pivot_longer(- genes,                         
               names_to = "sample", 
               values_to = "counts") %>% 
  filter(genes %in% diff_genes_Sd5vsd3_pos$genes) %>%  #using diff genes from Stampede: day 5 vs day 3           
  pivot_wider(names_from = "sample",            
              values_from = "counts")  %>%      
  column_to_rownames("genes")                   # the gene column is converted back to row names to create a matrix usable with pheatmap

dim(counts_normalised_only_diff_genes)          # check that you have the expected number of rows and 

#Scaling
counts_scaled = 
  counts_normalised_only_diff_genes %>% 
  t(.) %>%                              # transpose to have the genes in columns 
  scale() %>%                           # scale(x, center = TRUE, scale = TRUE) 
  t(.)                                  # back in original shape

# sanity check
# the majority of the values should be around zero
apply(counts_scaled, MARGIN = 1, mean) %>%                          # calculate the mean per row
  hist(., main = "", xlab = "Z-score values", col = "dodgerblue2") 

head(counts_scaled)
library(pheatmap)
pheatmap(counts_scaled, 
         cluster_rows = TRUE,                      
         cluster_cols = TRUE, 
         show_rownames = FALSE, 
         show_colnames = TRUE,
         main = "Clustering of differential genes")


counts_scaled_filtered = 
  counts_scaled %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>%
  dplyr::select(sampledata2$sample) # keep the 12 samples

head(counts_scaled_filtered)
colnames(counts_scaled_filtered)




#Annotated heatmap
anno_col_info = sampledata #%>% column_to_rownames("sample")
head(anno_col_info)
rownames(anno_col_info)
anno_col_info <- anno_col_info[,c("Genotype","Condition")]


#Check the data type
str(anno_col_info)
anno_info_colors = list(
  Genotype = c(Stampede = "burlywood", 
               Redhawk = "brown4"),
  Condition = c("day_5" = "black", 
                "day_3" = "lightgrey")
)


de_heatmap <-pheatmap(counts_scaled_filtered, 
         cluster_rows = TRUE,                       
         cluster_cols = TRUE, 
         show_rownames = FALSE, 
         show_colnames = TRUE,
         annotation_col = anno_col_info,
         annotation_colors = anno_info_colors,
         main = "Clustering of differentially expressed genes")

de_heatmap
```
